extracted.intended_audience: Congressional staff, Department of the Interior / Bureau of Indian Affairs officials, tribal leaders and legal/policy advisors working on federal recognition of Indian tribes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures for federal recognition of Indian tribes: evidentiary/definition factors, procedural protections (appeals, petition resubmission, burden of proof), membership/roll requirements, funding/appropriations, and consultation/notification obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case determination of service needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Each petitioning tribe should be assessed individually to determine the scope and range of services it needs; "we would look to each tribe on a case-by-case basis and determine the scope of services each tribe would need. All tribes obviously would not be entitled to all services."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department of the Interior expects factual circumstances and attributes of each group to vary and to dictate services; examples include a tribe without a land base not needing realty or forestry services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedure for disputes over service eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If a tribe recognized by the Secretary requests services for which they are found not eligible, there must be an appeal procedure: "They would be able to appeal the decision by the usual appeal route."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes use of established administrative appeal routes to resolve disputes about eligibility for particular services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioners must submit membership lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioning groups are required to submit a list of all current members of the group and a copy of each available former list of members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a requirement in the regulations; intended to support accountability and to let the Bureau know whom they are serving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department should maintain membership lists for accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Though not required for currently recognized tribes, the Department of the Interior believes membership lists are needed to assure Congress and the Bureau that a tribal government exists and to know who is being served.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCAI and witnesses stressed membership lists would improve accountability and administration of services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding assistance for tribes to prepare petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill/committee should provide funds or contracting authority to assist tribes in conducting the expensive legal and historical research required for petitions: "it would be far better if the bill included a provision that actually made funds available to the tribes for conducting their own research."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend a contracting provision similar to the Indian Self-Determination Act (P.L. 93-638) to allow Departments to contract with tribes for petition-preparation work; recognizes private support is not guaranteed and research is costly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget planning / specify financial burden of recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions should specify the financial burden recognition will place on the United States so Congress and funding authorities can plan appropriations; bill language indicates Congress shall not diminish services to existing tribes by recognizing new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee witnesses note that without notice of expected costs, Congress cannot prepare budgets or appropriate additional funds; this protects existing tribes' services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission of petitions allowed only with new evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups may resubmit petitions, but resubmission should be permitted only when new or additional evidence is presented that could not have been presented in the prior petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tomaskin supports resubmission only when demonstrably new evidence exists; avoids endless repeating of identical petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribal roll requirement and suggested blood-quantum baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Every newly recognized tribe must establish a tribal roll; suggested provision that every new roll be based on at least one-quarter Indian blood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposal aligns with National Tribal Chairmen's Association position; offered as a way to define membership and prevent ambiguity about who constitutes the tribe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof allocation for tribal status
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill provision places the burden on the Secretary of the Interior to prove that a group is not a tribe; some witnesses argue this burden should not rest on the Secretary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a contested procedural rule: the allocation of burden (Secretary must prove not-a-tribe vs. petitioners must prove they are a tribe) has significant practical and political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/Legal/Political evidence criteria (traditional factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition criteria should include valid, consistent factors such as historical, legal, and political evidence of tribal existence and continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses reference factors historically used (Indian Reorganization Act/1934 factors) and suggest such evidence must be central to any criteria; existing tribes should determine membership and not be forced to accept new groups without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five historical factors from Indian Reorganization Act (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors used in the past (under the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934) include: (1) treaty relations with the United States; (2) designation as a tribe by act of Congress or Executive order; (3) treatment as having collective rights on tribal lands or funds even if not expressly designated a tribe; (4) treatment as a tribe or band by other Indian tribes; (5) exercise of political authority over members through a tribal council or other governmental forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee and witnesses cite these as precedent-based evidentiary factors; they used them to criticize differences in Section 5 of the bill and to urge revision to align with prior practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only groups meeting established criteria may be recognized
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition should be limited to tribes or groups that satisfy the criteria established pursuant to agreed principles: "Only those tribes or groups who satisfy criteria to be established pursuant to principle may be recognized."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to prevent indiscriminate recognition and protect the significance of federal recognition and tribal sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear justification required for determinations of non-tribal status
rubrics_metrics.description: Every determination that a group is not an Indian tribe must be clearly justified on the group's failure to meet legitimate criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a requirement for reasoned decisions and transparency in denials of recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition must carry full legal force and not impair others' status
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition must carry all the force and impact of recognition by treaty, legislation, or administrative action, and "shall not negate or affect in any way the previous recognition . . . nor affect or dilute tribal assets or existing reservations . . . without the consent and approval of the already federally recognized tribe."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects existing tribes' rights and assets; new recognition cannot be used to diminish or alter prior recognitions or property without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional appropriations to meet obligations for newly recognized tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: When additional tribes are confirmed, the federal government should appropriate funds above and beyond operating levels presently received by currently recognized tribes; recognition should not force current tribes to absorb costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle stresses federal trust obligations and that budgetary constraints should not be the determinant of who receives recognition; also suggests Congress be prepared to appropriate additional funds on tribes' requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards must be consistent, valid, and protect tribal sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a valid and consistent set of criteria to frame petitions for recognition that protect tribal sovereignty and status; standards should provide necessary safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCAI and witnesses expressed that the bill's standards as written may be inadequate and urged development of standards around the 12 principles adopted by NCAI, with tribal consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation with tribes in developing regulations/standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards and regulations for recognition should be developed in consultation with tribal organizations and tribal leaders (e.g., NCAI), rather than unilaterally imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses urged the Committee and Department to work with tribal groups to craft acceptable criteria; Chairman invited collaboration with tribal staff and leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification and information obligations upon recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon recognition, the United States should inform the tribe of the rights, benefits, and protections afforded by federal Indian law; federal agencies should be prepared to fulfill trust obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also ties to congressional appropriations: tribes should be informed and Congress should appropriate additional funds as requested to meet obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect existing tribes from diminution of services
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of new tribes should not diminish services provided to previously recognized tribes; appropriations and planning must prevent slicing existing federal support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated concern of witnesses: indiscriminate recognition without additional appropriations risks reducing services and damaging all tribes' welfare.
